The experimental apparatus consists of a rotating blade model that simulates the leading edge geometry of a real turbine blade.
The blade model is electrically heated and cooled by impinging jets of refrigerant gas (Freon 12).
The local heat transfer coefficients are determined from the measured electrical input power and the skin temperature distribution.
The test section geometry includes a span of 101.6 mm, hub radius of 406.4 mm, tip radius of 508.0 mm, and leading edge diameter of 12.7 mm.
The impingement hole diameter is 2.1 mm and the hole pitch is 6.1 mm.
The tests were conducted at stagger angles of -30 degrees and 0 degrees.
The average jet Reynolds number varied from 17,000 to 74,000 in the tests.
Rotation reduces the mean Nusselt numbers by about 30% compared to non-rotating cases.
The thermal gradients between the jet holes along the passage are more pronounced at higher rotational speeds.
The heat transfer rates are lower by approximately 30% at 0 degree stagger angle compared to 30 degree stagger angle.
The maximum difference between Nusselt numbers calculated using local fluid temperature versus inlet coolant temperature is 17%.
The modeling and analysis offer a means for more accurate prediction of impingement cooling heat transfer rates.
The study provides insights into the effects of rotation and stagger angle on the local heat transfer distribution in turbine blade impingement cooling.
The channel flow model is used to correct the measured heat transfer coefficients to local fluid conditions.
The corrected results are compared to previous correlations for impingement cooling and rotating passages.
